reason: Section 32.2 contains distinct administrative-penalty topics: appointment and imposition, amount and notice requirements, admission and offence consequences, public and sentencing use, appeal exclusion, and repeat-penalty limits.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Administrative penalty Director, imposition, amount, notice, and limitation
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 32.2(1) through 32.2(5) establish the Director role, the power to impose a penalty by notice, the calculation and cap, required notice contents, and the three-year issuance limit.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who imposes administrative penalties, how amount and notice requirements work, and when a notice is time-barred.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Admission forms, payment, and offence-charge consequences
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 32.2(6) through 32.2(9) connect signed admissions and payment to deemed contravention, bar same-incident offence charges after payment, allow charges after non-payment, and prevent administrative penalties for the same incident once a person is charged.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how admission forms and payment affect deemed contravention, offence charges, and same-incident penalty liability.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Administrative penalty registry, sentencing use, no appeal, and repeat limit
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 32.2(10) through 32.2(13) address public access to signed admissions, later sentencing use, absence of appeal, and the limit on repeated substantially similar administrative penalties.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how administrative penalty admissions may be registered, disclosed, used at sentencing, insulated from appeal, and limited for repeat similar offences.

reason: Section 33 combines offence liability and fine rules with a separate evidentiary-document regime for prosecutions.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Offence liability, fine ranges, daily fines, and pesticide charges
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 33(1) through 33(3) identify what conduct is an offence, the fine ranges for individuals and others, the multiplier for continuing violations, and the charging rule for overlapping Pesticides Control Act offences.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Clean Environment Act offence, fine, continuing-violation, and Pesticides Control Act charging rules.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister documents and statements in offence prosecutions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 33(4) through 33(6) set evidentiary treatment for Minister documents, statements, and certified copies, plus notice and cross-examination requirements.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Minister documents and statements may be used in prosecutions and what notice and cross-examination protections apply.

reason: Section 33.01 is a cohesive enhanced-fine provision for offences committed for financial advantage or to avoid compliance costs, with a prosecutor notice prerequisite.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Enhanced fines for financial advantage or avoided compliance costs
proposedGroups.reason: The two subsections work together by authorizing fines beyond ordinary maxima in specified financial-benefit circumstances and requiring advance prosecutor notice.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a judge may impose an enhanced fine for financial advantage or avoided compliance costs and what notice must be given.

reason: Section 33.1 is a focused service provision identifying sufficient service methods for orders, notices, and other documents and deeming registered-mail service after five days.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Service methods and registered-mail deeming rule
proposedGroups.reason: The two subsections specify acceptable service methods and when service by prepaid registered mail is deemed effective.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how orders, notices, and other documents may be served and when registered-mail service is deemed effective.

reason: Section 33.2 is repeal-only and contains no current operative rule to author into a study group.
Section 34 is a single offence-classification rule making every non-individual who commits an offence under the Act or regulations subject to absolute liability.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Absolute liability for non-individual offenders

evidenceText: Every person other than an individual who commits an offence under this Act or the regulations commits an absolute liability offence

proposedGroups.reason: The target contains one rule about the liability classification for non-individual offenders.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a non-individual who commits an offence under the Act or regulations commits an absolute liability offence.

reason: Section 35 is a single limitation-period rule for proceedings in respect of offences under the Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Two-year limitation period for offence proceedings

evidenceText: Proceedings in respect to an offence under this Act may be instituted at any time within two years

proposedGroups.reason: The target contains one time limit measured from when the subject matter of the proceedings arose.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the two-year period for instituting Clean Environment Act offence proceedings.

reason: Section 36 is a single remedial rule allowing contraventions of the Act, regulations, or specified Minister or Lieutenant-Governor in Council instruments to be restrained in an action by the Minister.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Minister action to restrain contraventions

evidenceText: Where any provision of this Act or the regulations
in addition to any other remedy and to any penalty
may be restrained in an action at the instance of the Minister

proposedGroups.reason: The target identifies the contraventions that can be restrained and confirms the remedy is additional to other remedies and penalties.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Minister may bring an action to restrain contraventions of the Act, regulations, or specified instruments.

reason: Section 37 is a single preservation rule stating that civil remedies are not suspended or affected merely because the same act or omission is an offence under the Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Civil remedies unaffected by Act offences

evidenceText: No civil remedy for any act or omission is suspended or affected
by reason that the act or omission is an offence under this Act

proposedGroups.reason: The target contains one legal-effect rule preserving civil remedies despite offence status.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a civil remedy is not suspended or affected because an act or omission is also an offence under the Act.

reason: Section 38 is a transitional continuity rule deeming Water Act instruments to have been issued under the Act and continuing them until changed by the Minister.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Continuity of Water Act instruments under the Clean Environment Act

evidenceText: given, made or issued pursuant to the provisions of the Water Act
shall be deemed to have been given, made or issued
until revoked, suspended or varied by the Minister

proposedGroups.reason: The target gives continuing effect to Water Act orders, directions, requirements, licences, permits, approvals, and authorizations under the Clean Environment Act.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Water Act instruments are deemed and continued under section 38 until revoked, suspended, or varied.

reason: Clean Water Act section 1 is a large definitions section. Its defined terms support separate study groups for water and environmental media, authorizations and officials, contaminant and waste concepts, and water supply or infrastructure concepts.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Water and environmental media definitions
proposedGroups.reason: These definitions identify the environmental media, water bodies, watercourse features, watershed concepts, and wetlands used across the Clean Water Act.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Clean Water Act definitions for air, animal, aquifer, body of water, environment, ground water, surface water, watercourses, waters of the Province, watersheds, and wetlands.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Authorization, official, and procedural definitions
proposedGroups.reason: These definitions establish the Act's official roles, authorization instruments, monitoring concept, local-government meaning, and order terminology.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Clean Water Act meanings of analyst, inspector, Minister, monitoring, order, local government, and authorization instruments such as approvals, licences, permits, and registrations.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Contaminant, pollution, and waste definitions
proposedGroups.reason: These terms define contaminant-related risks, waste streams, wastewater infrastructure, and sources used in Clean Water Act controls.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Clean Water Act meanings of contaminant, danger of pollution, domestic wastewater, industrial waste, pesticide, sewer, solid waste, source of contaminant, storm water, and wastewater treatment facility.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Drinking water, wells, water supply, and works definitions
proposedGroups.reason: These definitions focus on drinking-water supply, wells, public systems, waterworks, and recognized fording places.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Clean Water Act meanings of potable water, private well, public water supply system, recognized fording place, water supply system, waterworks, and well.

reason: Clean Water Act section 2 is a single application rule binding both the Crown in right of Canada and the Crown in right of the Province to the Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Crown bound by the Clean Water Act

evidenceText: The Crown in right of Canada and the Crown in right of the Province are bound by the provisions of this Act

proposedGroups.reason: The target contains one rule identifying the Crown entities bound by the Act.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that both the federal and provincial Crown are bound by the Clean Water Act.

reason: Clean Water Act section 3 is a cohesive conflict-of-law provision stating the Act's general priority, the Public Health Act exception, and the validity of measures that could also have been taken under the Clean Environment Act.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Clean Water Act priority, public health exception, and Clean Environment Act overlap
proposedGroups.reason: The subsections work together to resolve conflicts with other legislation, carve out public-health matters, and preserve Clean Water Act measures despite Clean Environment Act overlap.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Clean Water Act conflicts are resolved, when the Public Health Act prevails, and why Clean Water Act measures remain valid despite Clean Environment Act overlap.

reason: Clean Water Act section 4 is a large order-power provision with separate target-supported topics for contaminant-release directions, triggering circumstances, possible recipients, compliance orders, facility order contents, order form and scope, compliance responsibility and access, duration, appeal effect, and successor binding.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Water contaminant-release order directions
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 4(1) lists the directions the Minister may include in an order responding to contaminant releases into or upon water.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the release control, investigation, reporting, cleanup, and remedial directions that may be ordered for contaminants released into or upon water.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Circumstances for water contaminant-release orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 4(2) separately states the Ministerial opinions and release circumstances that can support a contaminant order under the Clean Water Act.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the release-rate, prohibited-release, and public-interest circumstances that may justify a water contaminant order.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Persons who may receive water contaminant orders
proposedGroups.reason: Subsection 4(3) is a distinct list of possible recipients of a subsection 4(1) contaminant-release order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who a Clean Water Act contaminant-release order may be directed to.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Compliance orders and facility order contents
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 4(4) and 4(5) cover compliance orders for violations or failures to comply and the additional information and schedule requirements that may be included in wastewater treatment facility or waterworks orders.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Minister may issue a Clean Water Act compliance order and what information or schedule may be included in facility orders.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Order scope, written reasons, compliance responsibility, and access
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 4(6) through 4(9) govern order scope, writing and reasons outside emergencies, each directed person's responsibility and expense, and access needed to implement an order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Clean Water Act orders may cover multiple contaminants or persons and how writing, reasons, responsibility, expense, entry, and access rules operate.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Order duration, appeal effect, and successor binding
proposedGroups.reason: Subsections 4(10) through 4(12) state how long an order lasts, that an appeal does not suspend compliance, and who remains bound by the order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a Clean Water Act order ends, why appeal does not remove compliance, and how it binds heirs, successors, executors, administrators, and assigns.

reason: Clean Water Act section 5 is a focused follow-up order and non-compliance provision, covering additional remedial orders when existing action is inadequate and Ministerial entry to effect compliance after failure or refusal.

proposedGroups.titleSuggestion: Additional remedial orders and action after non-compliance
proposedGroups.reason: Both subsections address what the Minister may do after existing action is inadequate or a directed person fails or refuses to comply with an order.
proposedGroups.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Minister may order further remedial action or enter premises to effect compliance with a Clean Water Act order.
